text:
[what] — the change, in the imperative and concrete: which artifact, which
behaviour now differs. Not "improved things" — "extract _cycle_rollup, cmd_cycle
152 to 80 lines". The subject line is the headline; [what] is the precise diff in
one or two sentences. The gate requires [what] present (amber if missing).

[why] — the trigger and the decision. What task or breakage forced this, and —
when a fork was taken — which option was chosen and why the others were not. This
is where a design decision (canon vs template, fix vs leash, the residuality
verdict) is recorded so the next session inherits the reasoning, not just the
outcome. A [why] that only restates [what] wasted the block.

[how] — the mechanism and the key insight: the approach that worked and WHY it
worked when the obvious one did not. The one line that saves the next session
thirty minutes of re-discovery lives here ("sensor cursors are STRINGS, not
dicts"). Mechanism, not narration of every edit.

[test] — the verification evidence, replayable not quotable: the command run and
its result/exit code, re-run AFTER the last edit (§verify-never-claim). "smoke
green; unit 51 passed; doctor clean; index emits 1 commit-protocol chunk". An
EMPTY [test] block is a verify-never-claim violation in writing — the gate warns
on a [test] that reads like a claim ("should work") rather than evidence.

[broke] — the journey: what was tried and FAILED, and the real error text
verbatim (never paraphrased — the exact string grep would find). Dead ends are
the most valuable lines in the message: "Approach 1 failed because X" stops the
next session repeating it. Empty only when nothing failed — and be honest,
something usually does.

[next] — the baton: the single most important thing the next session should do,
and any state still broken or deferred. A deferred shortcut names its follow-up
task id here (§no-quick-fixes-without-a-leash). This is what the next session
reads first.

Never commit without the journey. "fix: resolved error" is worthless — what
error, what caused it, what was tried first. Every session starts from zero;
re-discovery is the number-one time killer. The commit that records the dead end
is the one that saves the next session from walking into it.

Paste real error messages, verbatim — the exact string grep would find, the
signal line not the full stack trace, never a paraphrase. A paraphrased error is
ungreppable and therefore lost. This is the same rule as §verbatim-protocol
applied to the log: the exact text carries signal a summary destroys.

Record what failed and why. "Approach 1: used RunRequest with partition_key
directly to ERROR: requires asset_selection" prevents the next agent from trying
it. Honesty over tidiness: a clean message that hides two failed approaches has
thrown away the most useful thing the session learned.

One logical change per commit — atomic. Do not mix a doc edit, a bug fix, and an
infra change in one commit. Each commit is a single reversible unit; mixing them
makes [broke]/[next] ambiguous and makes a clean revert impossible.

Verification is non-negotiable: every commit records what was checked and whether
it passed, in [test], re-run after the final edit. Evidence from a different
session or from before the last change does not count (§verify-never-claim). The
[test] block is the contract the commit-msg gate checks for evidence shape.

The log is queryable institutional memory. `git log --grep` mines it: by error
string to find who hit it before, by scope to see a subsystem's whole journey, by
"[broke]" to find every commit where something failed first. Writing the blocks
well is what makes these queries return signal years later.

The commit-msg gate (`socom gate commit-msg`) is the mechanical floor: subject
`type(scope): description` is RED (blocks), and missing [what] or [test] is amber
(warns + logs a breach, never blocks) — velocity-first, the safe path stays the
easy path (§psychological-acceptability). The four soft blocks ([why] [how] [broke]
[next]) are deliberately NOT hard-checked: their value is judgement, not presence,
and a gate that blocked on them would be routed around. This protocol documents
their meaning so they are written well; the gate guarantees only the floor.

No task is done until concrete proof is shown. "It should work" is a
violation: run the check, paste the output. Evidence from a different
session, or from before the final change, does not count — re-run after the
last edit. Evidence is replayable, not quotable: record the command and exit
code, not just the prose. If verification is impossible from here, state
explicitly what remains unverified and who must check it.

The validation contract — falsifiable acceptance checks with named assessors
— is written and ratified before implementation begins. Tests confirm
contracts; they are never retrofitted to bless whatever was built. A worker
cannot amend its own contract; renegotiation goes back to the originator and
is deliberately cheaper than bypass. Research-shaped work uses an exploration
promise: contract the question and a timebox, not an artifact.

Plan before coding for anything non-trivial: multi-file, architectural,
unfamiliar systems, unclear root cause. Prefer official docs, upstream
repositories, and specifications over guessing; never rely on unverified
forum answers. Store what you learn — memory or runbook — so research is
never repeated.

Every initiative's objective is to make an entire class of problem
structurally impossible at the root — never to patch the visible symptom.
State objectives in that form first: "eliminate class X by changing Y at the
root." When something is live and broken: mitigate the instance fast, but the
objective remains the class, same session.

Before proposing any fix or hard-to-reverse decision, run the 60-second
adversarial check: does this relocate stress rather than remove it? hide a
quantitative assumption? patch a symptom instead of the class? open a one-way
door? Trigger words that demand the gate: pin, bump, raise the limit, add a
retry, add a buffer, bigger node, works for now, temporarily, good enough.

No manual change to a live system that is not first — or same-session —
declarative in git. Temporary live patches reconcile in the same session; a
break-glass without same-session reconciliation is itself a new P0.
Operational state (tasks, handoffs, memories, lessons) lives in the repo:
any clone on any machine has the full state. Drift is a P0.

Outage time is a first-class cost. Rapid read-only diagnosis, then the
narrowest possible mitigation, then the permanent class-level fix — in that
order, in the same session. Do not delay live recovery to design the ideal
solution.

The primary's context is the scarcest resource. Offload bulk, mechanical,
and fan-out work to subordinate seats whose success is verifiable from
output (a count, a diff, a passing check). Retain judgment and final
verification in the primary — assessment is never delegated to the promiser.

Every brief to another participant opens with the originating human's words
verbatim — typos preserved, they carry signal — followed by the decoded
interpretation, clearly labeled, so the recipient can compare the two and
flag drift. Never verbatim credentials or personal data; redact before any
substrate write.

Every change must be one you would accept in the codebase a year from now.
An unavoidable shortcut gets three things: a documented why, a follow-up
task with an ID, and a TODO carrying that ID. A shortcut without a leash is
a violation, not a pragmatic call.

One commit format, enforced by hook: `type(scope): description` followed by
`[what] [why] [how] [test] [broke] [next]` blocks. Write full blocks on the
first branch commit — squash merges inherit it. The [test] block carries the
verification evidence; an empty [test] block is a verify-never-claim
violation in writing.
Scoping any initiative; answering "what's next" at session start; suspecting false-done.

One capability per initiative, one falsifiable exit per capability, tiers per
increment: T0 substrate missing → T1 present but not wired → T2 wired but not
tested → T3 tested but not shipped → T4 shipped but not adopted. The ladder is
O(1) orientation — next work is always the lowest tier whose exit is not
provably green — and a false-done detector: closure-orientation cannot mask
incomplete work when every tier has a command-verifiable exit.
Breaking an objective into sessions of work; sizing what one session may promise.

An initiative carries one falsifiable goal and a single success metric — "fix
class X at root Y" form (constitution §fix-the-class). Increments are the
rungs it ships on: each is a vertical slice that leaves the system whole and
provably one tier higher, never a horizontal layer that leaves everything
half-wired. An increment that cannot state its exit check is not yet an
increment; it is an intention.
Any fix spanning systems or layers; before implementing a ratified design; when a green check feels too easy.

Every session moves the system forward in unison: a change that fixes its
target while fragmenting the whole fails, even when its code is clean,
reviewed, and verified. Run the premise-check BEFORE executing: "which engine
already owns this responsibility?" A parallel mechanism beside an existing
owner is fragmentation with extra steps. Distrust the green live-proof that
only shows the symptom gone; trade-offs that bend another component get an
explicit follow-up task, never silence.
Closing any phase, task, or fix; reading a design doc that says "X happens"; inheriting a prompt's claims.

Two distinct gaps, both fatal to trust. A ratified decision is prose recording
intent — grep the implied code path and run the live operation before treating
it as built. And shipped code that works is still not accepted until the class
has a structural guard: ask "if we removed this code, does the class
reappear?" — if yes, the fix is isolated, not accepted; it needs a gate, a
type, a contract, or a check that makes recurrence impossible.
Any work spanning more than one layer or component; before dispatching builders.

No implementation begins until the artifact set exists: solution design,
implementation design, diagram, and contract — design-reviewed and
operator-ratified. The same set gates ready-to-close. Sizing is proportional
to scope (a small fix still surfaces design + diagram, briefly), but the gate
itself never waives: it pays for itself the first time review catches a false
invariant before code exists.
Organizing domains; naming things; deciding where work or data belongs; noticing the same word meaning two things.

A domain is a DDD bounded context: a boundary inside which every term has
exactly one agreed meaning (the ubiquitous language) and one owning team.
Boundaries are structural, not tags — things do not migrate casually across
them, and a domain that accepts everything is a dumping ground that defeats
the purpose. In the substrate itself, domains scope claims, lessons, and
buckets; in systems you build, they scope ownership and governance.
Two components or products sharing data about the same entity; any breaking-change dispute; coupling decisions.

A domain publishes a canonical definition of each shared entity; consumers
couple to declared semantic intent ("requires: customer_classification"),
never to internals like column names. The contract is validated structurally
at deploy/merge time and evaluated on upstream change as holds, stale, or
broken — broken blocks, with an event, not a surprise six months later. This
is the use-promise (−) made mechanical: downstream relies only on what
upstream promised, and the platform enforces the reliance.
Drawing deployment or ownership boundaries; deciding what "one unit" of a system is.

The smallest independently deployable unit with high functional cohesion,
carrying everything its function needs: logic, contract, metadata,
infrastructure declaration. "Independent" means an independent lifecycle and
ownership — not necessarily isolated runtime. In socom, the promise is the
quantum of work; in data platforms, the data product is the quantum of
architecture; both compose into aggregates without surrendering autonomy.
Designing any validation; deciding WHERE a failure should surface; consumer-facing errors that trace to producer omissions.

Move validation to the altitude where the person who can fix it meets it: a
product missing classification fails at the owner's publish step with an
actionable message — never as a consumer's read-time 500. By the time anything
is visible to a consumer it is safe-to-share by construction. Generalized:
every gate should fire at the desk of whoever owns the fix, as early as that
desk allows (shift-left applied to governance).
Designing any failure path, fallback, degradation, or health check.

Degradation is designed, never discovered. Security concerns (auth, masking,
classification) fail CLOSED: refuse rather than degrade, a 404 over an
unmasked row. Quality concerns (freshness, completeness) fail OPEN: serve the
previous good version with degradation metadata rather than nothing. Every
external dependency names its fallback at design time; a dependency without a
declared posture is an undesigned outage.
Writing any goal, contract, exit criterion, or "definition of done".

"How will we know?" must answer with a command and an expected output — "when
[command] returns [result]" — never with "looks good" or "feels right". If the
success of work cannot be falsified, the work cannot be promised, assessed, or
handed off; reframe until it can. This is the doctrine that makes every other
gate possible.

Long-running forge operations (CI runs, merge checks) are watched BY
the agent — background loop or watcher — never framed back to the
human as "should I keep monitoring?". The human hears outcomes.

State queries (ci-status, mr-status) must hit the provider's API
directly. Provider CLIs that serve cached listings are bound through
their cache-free forms; a stale answer is worse than a slow one.

A push is not done at exit 0: after every push, query ci-status and
carry the result into the evidence. A push with a failing pipeline is
not "done" (constitution §verify-never-claim).

Credentials and token plumbing live in the binding (or the provider's
credential helper), never improvised per-session. If auth fails, fix
the binding — do not inline secrets into commands or files.
Push the current branch to the canonical remote, with whatever auth the provider needs.
Latest pipeline/workflow state for this repo — result, status, branch. Cache-free.
Queue the repo's primary pipeline on a branch (extra args pass through).
Block-and-poll a run to a terminal state, emitting transitions; used by background watchers per rule poll-yourself.
Open a merge/pull request from the current branch to the default branch (title from args).
State of open MRs/PRs for this repo — id, title, vote/check state. Cache-free.
Print the repo's web URL (for handoffs and humans).

Sync and sanity before any work: fetch + fast-forward main; hash-diff compiled views against canonical (drift = P0, residue R3); orphan reaper — expired claims, dead worktrees, handoff-less sessions (R12); surface pending CI failures.
Runs the repo's fast checks on the changed surface before any task may transition to done. The fast tier has a hard latency budget — a slow check is demoted to CI, never tolerated here.
Repo's medium checks plus the structured-commit format contract. Amber: a failed medium check warns and records; the commit proceeds but the breach is logged with a deadline (CI re-asserts at red).
Repo's full checks. Local bypass (--no-verify) is permitted for flow but never escapes re-assessment: CI runs the same gate at red.

Rolls the run ledger into a scored cycle and fails when the measured pass-rate is below the bound threshold (checks.eval -> `socom cycle --gate --threshold N`). Verify-never-claim made quantitative: a seat's promises are scored (pass@1/pass@k by seat), not just asserted done; repeated below-threshold cycles surface hotspots as lesson candidates.
The incorruptible floor (R1): every gate re-asserted, contract checks executed, evidence replayed. The merge is the real door; no participant — human, agent, or hook-less runtime — routes around it.

The closeout pipeline: handoff artifact written (done / undone / commands / exit codes / blockers); next-session prompt generated then claim-verified against the repo (VERIFIED / REWRITTEN / HYPOTHESIS per claim); memory distillation gate (cap 2, five checks incl. falsifiability); claims released; worktrees removed.

Does this relocate stress rather than remove it? A fix that moves load,
contention, or failure pressure to another component, layer, or future
session has not removed the stress — it has hidden it where the next
person meets it cold. Remove the stress at its source or name where it now lives.

Does this hide a quantitative assumption? "Raise the limit", "add a
buffer", "bigger node" all encode a number nobody wrote down. Surface the
assumption (what value, why, when it breaks) or the fix is a silent time bomb.

Does this patch the visible symptom instead of the class? If the same bug
can recur one field, tenant, or path over, the class is still open
(constitution §fix-the-class). Patch the instance to mitigate now; the
objective remains the class-level fix, same session.

Does this open a one-way door? A hard-to-reverse decision (schema, public
contract, deletion, migration) must fail safe, not into disaster — Saltzer's
core distinction. If reversing it is expensive or impossible, it earns a
design-review and an explicit rollback story before it lands.

These words demand the gate, every time: pin, bump, raise the limit, add a
retry, add a buffer, bigger node, works for now, temporarily, good enough.
Reaching for one is the signal that stress is being relocated, not removed.

Keep the mechanism as small and simple as possible — what cannot be
inspected cannot be trusted. SOCOM: lean canon, "port the pattern, not the
code", §context-economy. Fail it when a change adds mechanism it cannot justify.

Base decisions on permission, not exclusion: a design error should deny, not
grant. SOCOM resolves the velocity tension by altitude — gates fail OPEN
locally (warn, exit 0) but fail CLOSED in CI where the fixer meets them (the
published-gate doctrine). Fail it when an error path grants instead of refusing.

Check every access to every object, including at init, recovery, shutdown,
maintenance. SOCOM: gates at every band — session-start, task-completion,
pre-commit, pre-push, ci, session-end. Fail it when a path skips the check.

Security must not depend on secrecy of the mechanism. SOCOM: §git-is-source-of-truth,
the open seat registry, the L0 grep floor — the whole substrate is inspectable.
Fail it when correctness relies on something hidden or unwritten.

Require two keys, not one. SOCOM: builder and reviewer never share context; a
worker cannot amend its own contract; assessment is never delegated to the
promiser. Fail it when one actor can both act and bless the action.

Every actor operates with the minimum privilege its function needs. SOCOM:
domain-scoped claims with TTL auto-expiry, isolated worktrees, bounded seat
promises. Fail it when a change grants more reach than the task requires.

Minimize mechanism shared across actors — shared state is a coupling and an
information path. SOCOM: an isolated worktree per session, never the shared
checkout. Fail it when a change forces unrelated work through one shared point.

Make the protected path the easy path, or people route around it. SOCOM:
velocity-first — gates warn-not-block locally precisely so they are never
disabled. Fail it when the safe path is so painful it invites bypass.

Weigh the cost of doing it right against the cost of going around. SOCOM
inverts it: renegotiating a contract is deliberately CHEAPER than bypassing it.
Fail it when the wrong path is the cheap path.

When you cannot prevent, record — a detectable breach beats a silent one.
SOCOM: the breach ledger (`socom breach`), amber gates that warn-and-log and
feed trust scoring. Fail it when a fail-open path leaves no trace.

Running the residuality gate records, in the commit [test]/[why] or the design
note: (1) the trigger that fired (a trigger-word, a fix, a hard-to-reverse
decision); (2) which gate questions and Saltzer principles the change was tested
against; (3) the verdict — passes / relocates-stress / hides-an-assumption /
symptom-only / opens-a-one-way-door; (4) the resolution, or — if a shortcut was
knowingly accepted — the documented why and the follow-up task id that leashes it
(constitution §no-quick-fixes-without-a-leash). A gate run with no recorded verdict
did not happen.
Owns decomposition and dispatch. Publishes intents and validation contracts, decomposes initiatives into promises, assigns seats. Never writes production code.
Implements one contracted unit of work in an isolated worktree, self-checks against the contract, and submits evidence. The default production seat.
Independent adversarial assessor. Judges a builder's promise against the ratified contract and repo conventions, from clean context. Its promise is honest assessment, not approval.
Verifies the live effect against the contract on the deployed/running system — not the diff. Drives the real thing and records observed behavior as evidence.
Bounded research on a specific question; returns a compact, decision-ready brief. Stores durable findings as reference memories.
Produces objective structural telemetry — dependency graphs, hotspots, coupling, coverage — measurements, not advice.
Competing-hypothesis investigation: multiple heads each champion a different theory and actively try to disprove the others. For debugging with unclear root cause.
Non-coding engineering seat: produces ratified ADRs, runbooks, and documentation through the same contract/assessment loop builders use for code.
Agentic retrieval seat (evolution L3): promises decision-ready context — decomposes the question, walks the link graph, assesses freshness, returns a briefed bundle with provenance.

1. Fetch + fast-forward main. Create an isolated worktree — never work in
   the shared checkout. Run the orphan reaper (expired claims, dead
   worktrees, handoff-less sessions).
2. Discover the latest next-session prompt AND run the drift scan — the
   prompt states what was true at write time; the repo states what is true
   now. Surface every mismatch before planning.
3. Claim the work: register the promise against a bucket row and its
   contract.
4. Load the retrieval map's session-start section and the lessons for the
   task's domain.
5. Non-trivial work enters plan mode; the plan is ratified against the
   contract before any code.

Contract first if none exists. Implement; run the fast gate after every
change. Dispatch seats with verbatim briefs; builder and reviewer never
share context. Run the residuality gate before any fix lands. Capture
memory/lesson candidates as they occur — distillation happens at closeout,
recall is not trusted.

One uninterrupted pipeline: bucket rows flipped to reality → push → CI
verified green → handoff written (done / undone / commands / exit codes /
blockers / warnings) → next-session prompt generated then claim-verified →
memory distillation (cap 2, five gates) → claims released, worktrees
removed, clean process table.
evals extraction: socom cycle (ledger->cycle measurement spine) + next-session prompt id/timestamp

Two increments, all gates green, pushed to origin/main, CI verified green
(run 27480499785 -> success).

1. next-session prompt identity (4181b81, 6af363a): `socom prompt` now stamps
   every generated prompt with id=P-<date>-<branch> +
   generated=<ts> + source-handoff, inherited from the handoff (single
   ordering authority, no second clock). .socom/prompts/ is now tracked.
   Smoke locks the header. WHY: the session-start drift scan needs a
   write-time IN the prompt, not git mtime.

2. evals extraction = backlog #1 (c405560, 095a923): the ledger->cycle
   measurement spine, the first Akili->SOCOM port.
   - schemas/ledger.xml: append-only JSONL run ledger (.socom/ledger/runs.jsonl),
     one row per promise execution (seat, promise, contract, gate_band,
     exit_code, duration_s, attempt, verdict kept|broken).
   - `socom cycle`: rolls the ledger into a scored cycle — pass@1/pass@k BY
     SEAT, hotspots, exit-codes, attempts, contract-coverage. Flags
     --since/--seat/--cycle/--gate --threshold. Read-only, cache-free,
     degrades loudly with no ledger.
   - `eval` gate (canon/gates.xml + .socom/canon/gates.xml) bound to
     checks.eval = `socom cycle --gate --threshold 70`; fails below threshold.
   - Gate dispatch generalized: unknown gate id -> checks.<id> (so canon
     can add gates with no new dispatch code); unknown-gate guard kept.
   - Renamed from the prompt's `socom eval` (collides with the existing L1
     retrieval-acceptance gate) to `socom cycle` — operator-ratified.

Contract (all 4 checks PASS, evidence in c405560 [test] block): ledger.xml
well-formed; seeded hand-count matches (builder 1/2 & 2/2, reviewer 0/1,
pass@1 1/3, pass@k 2/3); gate RED below / PASS above; doctor clean
(source=fce8a0829b46), compile idempotent. Full smoke green (9 new
cycle/gate assertions). CI green post-push.

Deliberately deferred (scope discipline — ONE increment): auto-append of
ledger rows from gates/closeout (MVP seeds by hand); the full query suite as
flags (health/trends/reliability); efficiency/journal-quality metrics;
amber-band measurement gating (eval gate is red for testable both-directions).
No ledger is wired to write yet — `socom cycle` works but nothing populates
.socom/ledger/runs.jsonl in normal operation. That wiring + the lessons
bridge are the next session.
None.

- canonical_hash() reads .socom/canon/, NOT canon/. Editing a canon file
  (e.g. gates.xml) requires syncing BOTH canon/ (shipped template) and
  .socom/canon/ (this repo's live canon) then `socom compile`, or doctor
  shows HR9 divergence / stale views. Cost a detour this session.
- `socom cycle` is built but no ledger is auto-populated yet — it will
  degrade-loud ("no ledger") until something appends runs. Expected.
- Pre-existing uncommitted churn left untouched on purpose: .socom/gates/
  breaches.log (amber breach records) and .socom/index/chunks.jsonl — not
  part of this work; sweep them deliberately or leave for their owner.

1. Backlog #2 — Lessons system: wire the cycle's hotspots (repeated
   broken promises) into lesson candidates; LESSON-SYSTEM-ENGINEERING.md is
   the Akili source. This is the natural continuation of evals.
2. Wire ledger auto-append: gates/closeout append a run row per promise
   execution so `socom cycle` measures real operation, not just seeds.
3. (smaller) cycle query flags: --health/--trends as read-only views.
contract verify (#6) + bin/socom self-maintenance SM-1/2/3

Two tracks shipped, gates green, all pushed + CI-verified green.

**Backlog #6 — Contract machinery** (commit 1b33918): `socom contract
verify|show`. The validation contract was doctrine + inert XML; verify now
EXECUTES each `<check><run>` command a promise embeds (schemas/promise.xml),
PASS/FAIL on exit code, and flags no-run checks MANUAL (fail-closed — never
auto-passed; the mechanical assessor never claims the human verdict). New
schemas/contract.xml (schema-by-example). Pure helpers _contract_el /
_contract_checks / _verify_summary, unit-tested. Reframe from research:
SOCOM already HAD the contract shape; #6 made it executable, not a new
notion. Sixth Akili->SOCOM extraction. Evidence: verify on a
true/false/no-run fixture -> PASS/FAIL/MANUAL, exit 1; pass+manual -> exit
0; unit 51 passed; smoke all green; doctor clean.

**Substrate self-maintenance SM-1/2/3** (operator-triggered: "bin for socom
py is not good quality... one monolithic script"). Analyst telemetry
reframed it (file is 91% IO; single-file is deliberate/load-bearing; real
debt = untested core + duplication + 3 hotspots).
- SM-1 (cd01bfe): tests/unit.py, white-box assertions on the pure core,
  chained into smoke+CI — the refactor safety net.
- SM-2 (eb7f490): SOCOM_DIR constant (52 magic strings) + _now_iso() (9
  stamps); die() residuality-REJECTED (lateral, risks smoke-grepped text).
- SM-3 (b9400bf): decomposed cmd_cycle (CC 61 -> the 4x outlier eliminated),
  extracted pure _cycle_rollup + 14 white-box tests; 152->80 lines.
Unit suite grew 0 -> 51 assertions; every step behaviour-preserving (doctor
clean = byte-identical compile, smoke green, each push CI-green).

#6 followups (backlog row 6f, deferred — NOT built, residuality: no sprawl):
standalone `.socom/contracts/<id>.xml` storage + lifecycle; §R10
renegotiation (new version + originator re-ratification + diff); record
verify results into the assertion log (#4 bridge) or auto-append a ledger
row; per-contract pass@1/pass@k in cmd_cycle.
SM-3 remainder (optional): cmd_gate (CC 39) + render_body (CC 23) — far
below the cmd_cycle outlier; decompose only if they bite. SM-4 (package +
bundler) stays deferred behind its one-way-door gate.
None.

- `socom contract verify` EXECUTES the contract's `<run>` commands via the
  shell in the repo context — by design (it is the verification runner), and
  the author of a ratified contract owns those commands, like any test. Do
  not point verify at an untrusted contract.
- This handoff OVERWROTE the prior H-2026-06-14-main.xml (which described #5
  + closeout). Tool design: one rolling handoff per day+branch; the #5
  detail is preserved in git history + commits f5bb53c/cb00b98. The SM-1/2/3
  increments shipped AFTER that #5 handoff were not yet captured — this
  refresh is what makes the handoff catch up to repo reality.
- .socom/index/chunks.jsonl shows modified: pre-push `full` runs `socom
  index .`; pre-existing non-stable-output churn, left untouched.
- Push + CI-verify still owed at write time (forge §verify-after-push).

1. Backlog #7 — commit-protocol -> canon (or socom.yaml): per-block
   [what][why][how][test][broke][next] semantics + templates (the #5
   deferred half). Decide canon-file vs socom.yaml/hook config at pickup.
2. Backlog #6f — contract followups: standalone storage, §R10
   renegotiation, verify->assertion/ledger recording, per-contract metrics.
3. Still open: ledger auto-append (cycle/lesson still synthetic) — #6f's
   "record verify -> ledger" would start closing this; precond bootstrap
   guidance; SM-3 remainder (cmd_gate/render_body) only if they bite.
two increments: commit-protocol to canon (#7) + contract verify --record, the first real ledger producer (#6f-1)

**Backlog #6f-1 — contract verify --record** (commit 927905d, pushed +

editing canon (gates/roles/etc) — which dir is authoritative, and the sync+compile step

`canonical_hash()` in `bin/socom` reads from `<repo>/.socom/canon/`, **not** the
top-level `canon/`. The two are distinct:

- `canon/` — the **shipped template** `socom init` copies into a new repo's `.socom/canon/`.
- `.socom/canon/` — **this repo's live canon**; it drives the source hash and all compiled views.

**How to apply:** when changing a canon file (e.g. adding a gate to `gates.xml`),
edit **both** `canon/<file>` (so adopters get it) and `.socom/canon/<file>` (so this
repo uses it — keep them byte-identical), then run `socom compile`. Editing only
`canon/` does nothing to this repo; editing only `.socom/canon/` silently diverges
from the shipped template (`socom doctor` flags it as HR9 divergence). After compile,
`socom doctor` must be clean and the new source hash propagates to CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md
/ .cursor / .githooks / CI adapters — commit all of them together or you get drift.

designing any SOCOM gate/check/pre-flight — the heal/warn/block posture that keeps velocity fast

Operator constraint for the substrate: **information velocity must stay fast AND
highest quality — a gate must never disrupt flow.** This is a design rule for
every gate, check, and pre-flight in SOCOM, not a one-off.

**The posture (in priority order):**
1. **Auto-heal** what is safely fixable (mkdir a dir, set a git config) — fix it
   inline, don't stop for it.
2. **Warn (amber)** by default — record + surface + proceed.
3. **Block (red)** ONLY on the genuinely unrecoverable (a missing tool, a
   destroyed precondition with healing disabled).
4. Keep it **fast band** (hard latency budget; print elapsed ms to prove it).
5. **Advisory > mandatory**: prefer a command the operator runs over a hard
   blocking gate; allow local bypass and let CI re-assert (`--no-heal` is the CI
   assert posture).
6. Surface the **exact fix at the altitude where it's met** (the published-gate
   doctrine) so resolution is instant.

`socom precond` (commit ea71c32) is the reference implementation of this posture.
`socom doctor` / the gate bands (amber warns, red blocks) follow the same spirit.
When adding a new gate, default to heal/warn; justify any red. Mirrors the
operator-feedback memory in the user bank. Related: [[canon-hash-reads-dot-socom]].
generating XML (templates/f-strings) — the '--' in comments trap that makes index silently skip files

**XML comments cannot contain `--` (double hyphen).** It is not just the `-->`
terminator — any `--` inside a `<!-- ... -->` block makes the document
not-well-formed (`ParseError: not well-formed (invalid token)`).

This bites when generating XML artifacts from f-string/templates whose comments
mention CLI flags: a lesson template comment read `socom lesson retire <id>
--reason ...`, and the `--reason` silently broke every generated `<lesson>`.

**Why it's nasty in SOCOM:** `socom index` (`bin/socom`, `rglob .socom/**.xml`)
catches `ET.ParseError` and **skips** the file with only a stderr line — so a
malformed artifact doesn't crash anything, it just **never reaches retrieval**.
The symptom is "my new artifact won't show up in `socom query`," not an error.

**How to apply:** never put `--` in an XML comment (reword flag examples:
`retire it with a reason` not `--reason`; `re-confirmed` not `-- confirmed`).
When a generated `.xml` artifact mysteriously isn't indexed, first run
`python3 -c "import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET; ET.parse('<file>')"` — a skip
in `socom index` stderr or a ParseError is the tell. Related: [[canon-hash-reads-dot-socom]].
